title: Everyday requests
tip: Stress the important words (nouns, verbs, adjectives) and say little words like 'to', 'a' and 'the' quickly and lightly.
items: Could you tell me where the station is?
I'd like a table for two, please.
Would you mind opening the window?
Can I have the bill, please?
I'm looking for a quiet place to work.
Do you know what time the shop closes?
Excuse me, is this seat taken?
Thanks a lot, that was really helpful.

title: Giving opinions
tip: Raise your pitch on the key word of your opinion and let your voice fall at the end of a statement.
items: In my opinion, the plan is too expensive.
I strongly believe that we should wait.
As far as I can see, there's no real problem.
It seems to me that both sides have a point.
I'm not convinced that it will work.
To be honest, I'd rather stay at home.
That's an interesting idea, but I disagree.
On the whole, I think it was a success.

title: Questions and intonation
tip: Wh-questions (what, where, why) usually fall at the end. Yes/no questions usually rise.
items: Where did you put the keys?
Are you coming to the meeting?
What time does the train leave?
Did you finish the report?
Why didn't you call me?
Is there anything else I can do?
How long have you lived here?
Would you like some tea or coffee?

title: Linking words together
tip: Native speakers join words: a consonant at the end of a word moves to the vowel that follows. 'Pick it up' sounds like 'pi-ki-tup'.
items: Pick it up and put it in a box.
Turn it off and take it away.
Come on in and sit down.
I'll call you in an hour.
Check out the new office on Main Street.
She has an interesting idea about it all.
Look at it again and again.
Find out if he is at home.

title: Weak forms and contractions
tip: Words like 'for', 'to', 'and', 'of', 'can' and 'have' are often reduced to a short 'uh' sound when they are not stressed.
items: I can do it for you.
She's been waiting for an hour.
We should have called him.
What do you want to do?
He could have told us about it.
I'll have a cup of tea and a piece of cake.
They've gone to the shops.
You must be joking.

title: Numbers, dates and times
tip: Say numbers clearly: 'thirteen' stresses the end, 'thirty' stresses the start. Dates use ordinal numbers.
items: The meeting starts at a quarter past nine.
It costs thirteen pounds and fifty pence.
My birthday is on the twenty-third of March.
There are thirty students in the class.
The flight leaves at seven forty-five.
She was born in nineteen ninety-eight.
Call me on zero seven eight one two.
It's about fifteen minutes away.

title: On the phone
tip: Speak a little slower than usual and stress names, numbers and key details so that they are easy to catch.
items: Hello, this is Sarah from the sales department.
Could I speak to Mr Khan, please?
I'm afraid he's not available right now.
Can I take a message?
Could you spell your surname for me?
I'll get back to you as soon as possible.
Thank you for calling, and have a nice day.
Sorry, the line is bad. Could you repeat that?

title: Job interview
tip: Sound confident: speak at a steady pace, pause at commas and let your voice fall at the end of statements.
items: I have five years of experience in marketing.
My greatest strength is working well in a team.
I'm looking for a role where I can grow.
In my previous job, I managed a team of six.
I'm particularly interested in the research side.
I'm a quick learner and I enjoy new challenges.
Could you tell me more about the company culture?
Thank you for taking the time to meet me.

title: Presenting
tip: Pause between ideas, stress the key words in each phrase and slow down for important numbers.
items: Today I'd like to talk about three main points.
Let me start with a brief overview.
As you can see on this slide, sales have doubled.
This brings me to my next point.
The results were significantly better than expected.
To sum up, the project was a success.
I'd be happy to answer any questions.
Thank you all for your attention.

title: Telling a story
tip: Vary your pitch to keep the listener interested: higher and louder for the surprise, slower for the suspense.
items: Last weekend something strange happened to me.
I was walking home when I heard a noise.
At first I thought it was the wind.
Suddenly, the lights went out.
I couldn't believe my eyes when I looked up.
It turned out to be a very friendly cat.
We both laughed about it afterwards.
The funny thing is, it followed me all the way home.

title: Polite disagreement
tip: Soften disagreement with a gentle start and a slightly higher, lighter voice, then give your reason.
items: I see what you mean, but I see it differently.
That's a fair point, however I'm not sure it's practical.
I'm afraid I can't agree with that.
With respect, I think we need more time.
I understand your concern, but let's look at the facts.
You may be right, although I have my doubts.
Could we perhaps consider another option?
Let's agree to disagree on this one.

title: Feelings and emotions
tip: Let your voice show the feeling: a wider pitch range sounds excited or surprised, a narrow, lower range sounds tired or serious.
items: I'm absolutely delighted with the results!
Honestly, I'm a bit disappointed.
That's wonderful news, congratulations!
I was so embarrassed when it happened.
She seemed rather worried about the exam.
I can't tell you how relieved I am.
He's furious about the delay.
What a lovely surprise to see you!

title: Stress changes meaning
tip: The word you stress shows what you mean. Try each sentence and notice how the meaning changes with the stressed word.
items: I didn't say he stole the money.
I never said she took the bag.
He told me that he was tired.
We can't afford a new car this year.
She only wanted a cup of tea.
I think you should apply for the job.
They didn't want to go to the party.
Just give me a minute.

title: English rhythm
tip: English has a steady beat on the stressed syllables. Unstressed syllables are squeezed in between, so 'cat sat mat' and 'the cat sat on the mat' take about the same time.
items: Cats eat mice.
The cat is eating the mouse.
The cats have been eating the mice.
Dogs chase cats.
The dogs were chasing the cats.
Buy some bread.
Could you buy some bread for me?
Could you have bought some bread for the family?
